$comment: Bridge presets offered by the Tor Bridge Settings screen.
DarkFlow deliberately ships no hard-coded bridge addresses. Bridge lines
are rotated by the Tor Project precisely because censors block them, so a
list baked into an app release is stale within weeks and gives users a
false sense of working access. Instead:
* the presets below select the pluggable transport and the torrc wiring,
* the app fetches bridges at runtime through BridgeDB's moat interface
when the network allows it (see tool/fetch_bridges.ps1 for the same
request made from a desktop shell),
* and the user can always paste their own lines into the manual box.
The `bridges` arrays are intentionally empty: an empty preset means
'use this transport, and obtain addresses from moat or from the user'.
Do not fill them with addresses copied from a blog post.

presets.label: No bridge
presets.description: Connect straight to the Tor network. Correct where Tor is not blocked; if the bar stops around 10%, come back and pick a transport.

presets.label: obfs4
presets.description: Traffic is scrambled so it resembles nothing recognisable. The most widely usable transport, and the one to try first.

presets.label: WebTunnel
presets.description: The connection looks like ordinary HTTPS to a website, which defeats blocks that only allow web browsing.

presets.label: Snowflake
presets.description: Routes through volunteers' browsers. No addresses to maintain, but slower and less predictable.

presets.label: meek
presets.description: Domain fronting through a large CDN. Slow, but it works in some of the most restrictive networks.

moat.$comment: The moat API requires solving a challenge for /request; /builtin returns the transports that need no addresses at all.
